title: Study designs and the evidence hierarchy
note: In an experiment, researchers assign the exposure; in an observational study, they only watch. Randomized controlled trials best support cause and effect. Cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies find associations. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses combine many studies and sit at the top of the evidence pyramid.

read.title: Why design matters
text: Suppose you want to know whether a new exercise program lowers blood pressure. In a cohort study, you would follow people who chose the program and people who didn't. If the exercisers end up healthier, you still can't be sure why. People who sign up for exercise may also eat better, smoke less, or have more free time.

A randomized controlled trial solves this by letting chance decide who gets the program. With enough participants, random assignment spreads diet, smoking, motivation and every other factor, measured or not, evenly across the groups. A difference at the end is then most plausibly caused by the program.

Trials are not always possible. You can't randomly assign people to smoke, and rare diseases would need enormous trials. Case-control studies start with people who already have the disease and look back at exposures, which makes them efficient for rare outcomes. Cross-sectional surveys give a quick snapshot of how common something is but can't show what came first.

Because single studies can mislead, systematic reviews gather every relevant study with a documented search, and meta-analyses pool their results. That is why they top the evidence pyramid, though a review built on weak studies is still weak.

q.q: Why can't the cohort study prove the exercise program caused the improvement?
o: People who chose the program may differ in other ways
The sample is always too small
Cohort studies never measure blood pressure

q.q: Why are case-control studies efficient for rare diseases?
o: They start with people who already have the disease
They measure everything on one day

q.q: What limits even a systematic review?
o: It never uses a documented search
It is only as strong as the studies it gathers
